text: Nov 25, 2026 · 8 min read Vivien Cheng , Jerry Liu , Morris Yau , Chris Ré The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) posits that neural networks converge toward a shared representation of reality. Prior work shows that separately trained models learn geometrically similar representations, but similar does not mean interchangeable . Can one LLM use another’s representations in place of its own, without gradient descent? Yes, and the map is surprisingly simple. A rotation and one global scale , fit in closed form, let one LLM use another’s representations. We demonstrate this on factual recall across 12 base LLMs from eight families ( 1.5B–27B parameters). For example, a recipient LLM prompted with “The capital of Germany is” answers “Berlin”. We take a donor LLM’s hidden state at “France”, rotate and scale it, and swap it in for the recipient’s state at “Germany”. The recipient’s answer flips to “Paris” ( Fig. 1 ). Extract. Take the donor’s hidden state at “France”. Map. Rotate and scale the state into the recipient’s representation space. Swap. Replace the recipient’s state at “Germany”. The recipient now answers “Paris” instead of “Berlin”. Our main findings: These findings point toward a shared, lower-dimensional structure across LLMs ( Fig. 6 ), opening up new research directions such as latent communication. Geometric similarity does not show whether one LLM can use another’s representations, so we test this directly on factual recall. Factual recall in LLMs resembles a key–value lookup : early-to-middle layers build a key at the last subject token (“France”), which later layers use to retrieve the value (“Paris”) from the weights. We swap the key rather than the value, leaving the recipient’s later layers to retrieve the answer. If this single hidden-state swap changes the answer to “Paris”, the representation has transferred. Our map aligns keys across frozen LLMs using only a rotation and one global scale , fit in closed form on fewer than 5,000 training facts that both LLMs recall. Let μ A ​ , μ B ​ be the mean keys and Z ~ A ​ , Z ~ B ​ the centered key matrices (one key per column) of the donor and recipient, respectively. We compute the orthogonal Procrustes rotation R via a thin SVD and choose the global scale s to roughly match the recipient’s overall spread: Here, “rotation” includes reflections and semi-orthogonal maps between different hidden dimensions. We test the map on 20 model pairs using 8,800 facts, each a subject and its answer under one of 16 relations, such as capitals and authors. Our 12 base LLMs span eight families ( 1.5B–27B parameters; Fig. 6 ). For each pair, we use only facts that both LLMs recall on their own. We measure transfer accuracy as the percentage of swaps that make the recipient generate the donor’s answer ( Fig. 1 ). We split facts by subject into training, validation, and test sets: we fit the map on training facts, select the swap layers ( ℓ A in the donor and ℓ B in the recipient) that maximize validation transfer accuracy, and report test results. Representations can be geometrically similar without being functionally interchangeable. Yet a simple change of coordinates lets one LLM use another’s representations. Rotations align pairs of LLMs, but do all LLMs share one underlying geometry? If so, a chain of rotations (A → B → C) should transfer nearly as well as a direct rotation (A → C). We also ask how many dimensions factual transfer needs ( Fig. 3 ). Chaining. A chain of rotations (A → B → C) retains a median 99% of the transfer accuracy of a direct rotation (A → C). Compression. A rotation fit on the top 256 principal components retains a median 74% of the full rotation’s transfer accuracy. With just 16 components, the median drops to 4%. Shared space? Both results are consistent with LLMs being rotated views of one shared, lower-dimensional space. Rather than a map for every pair, each LLM might need just one rotation into a shared, lower-dimensional space ( Fig. 6 ). So far, we have used rotations to change what an LLM recalls, but could we also use this shared geometry to rescue failed recall? Prior work shows that LLMs store facts they fail to recall, which we call dark memories . As a proof of concept, we use a rotated key from another LLM to unlock them ( Fig. 5 ). Own key. With its own key for “Interstellar”, the recipient answers “Denis Villeneuve”. Donor key. We swap in the donor’s rotated and scaled key for “Interstellar”. Unlock. The donor’s key retrieves the stored answer from the recipient’s memory: “Christopher Nolan”. Some failures of factual recall can be rescued by changing the key rather than the weights. A simple change of coordinates lets one LLM unlock another’s dark memories. A closed-form rotation and scale let one LLM use another’s representations for factual recall. We read this as functional evidence for the PRH : the representations are not just similar but partly interchangeable. This also fits our lab’s view of MLPs as Hebbian memories , and suggests that one LLM’s rotated keys can query another’s memory. We’re very excited to explore two directions: Twelve views. Each LLM has its own representation space. Align. Jointly fit a rotation and scale for each LLM. Shared space? If LLMs share one underlying geometry, corresponding representations should align.
